content.stem: A random sample of $400$ residents of a city was surveyed, and $62\%$ of them said they support building a new public library. The margin of error for this estimate is $5$ percentage points. Which conclusion is most appropriate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It is plausible that between $57\%$ and $67\%$ of all city residents support building the library.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Exactly $62\%$ of all city residents support building the library.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Between $57\%$ and $67\%$ of the $400$ surveyed residents support building the library.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It is likely that fewer than half of all city residents support building the library.

content.explanation: A random sample estimates the whole population, and the margin of error gives a range of plausible values for it. Subtracting and adding the margin of error gives $62\% - 5\% = 57\%$ to $62\% + 5\% = 67\%$ of all residents.

distractorRationales.label: B
distractorRationales.text: A sample gives an estimate with uncertainty, not an exact value for the population.

distractorRationales.label: C
distractorRationales.text: The percent for the 400 surveyed residents is known exactly, $62\%$; the margin of error applies to the whole population.

distractorRationales.label: D
distractorRationales.text: The entire plausible range, $57\%$ to $67\%$, is above $50\%$.

content.stem: A university has $12{,}000$ students. In a random sample of $150$ of these students, $36$ said they ride a bike to campus. Based on the sample, which is the best estimate of the number of students at the university who ride a bike to campus?
content.explanation: In the sample, $\frac{36}{150} = 0.24$, or $24\%$, ride a bike. Because the sample is random, apply this to all students: $0.24 \times 12{,}000 = 2{,}880$.

distractorRationales.label: A
distractorRationales.text: This is the number of bikers in the sample, not in the whole university.

distractorRationales.label: B
distractorRationales.text: This applies $24\%$ to $1{,}000$ students instead of $12{,}000$.

distractorRationales.label: D
distractorRationales.text: This is the estimated number of students who do not ride a bike: $12{,}000 - 2{,}880$.

content.stem: A town council wants to estimate the percent of all town residents who would use a new dog park. Which survey method is most likely to give an estimate that can be applied to all town residents?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Surveying $300$ people at a pet store in the town

choices.label: B
choices.text: Surveying $300$ residents chosen at random from a complete list of town residents

choices.label: C
choices.text: Posting a survey on the town's website and using the first $300$ responses

choices.label: D
choices.text: Surveying $300$ people walking dogs in the town's largest park

content.explanation: To apply a sample's results to a whole population, the sample should be chosen at random from that population, so every resident has the same chance of being picked. Choosing at random from a complete list of residents does that.

distractorRationales.label: A
distractorRationales.text: People at a pet store are more likely than typical residents to own pets and want a dog park.

distractorRationales.label: C
distractorRationales.text: People who choose to answer an online survey may care more about the issue than other residents.

distractorRationales.label: D
distractorRationales.text: People walking dogs are much more likely than typical residents to use a dog park.

content.stem: A researcher surveyed a random sample of $400$ adults in a state about their exercise habits and reported a margin of error for the estimate. The researcher plans to repeat the survey using a random sample of $1{,}600$ adults from the same state, with the same method. Compared with the first survey, the margin of error for the second survey will most likely be

choices.label: A
choices.text: larger, because more people means more variety in the answers.

choices.label: B
choices.text: smaller, because a larger random sample tends to give a more precise estimate.

choices.label: C
choices.text: the same, because the samples come from the same population.

choices.label: D
choices.text: zero, because $1{,}600$ adults is enough to know the population value exactly.

content.explanation: Larger random samples give estimates that tend to land closer to the true population value, so the margin of error shrinks as the sample size grows (with the same method and confidence level).

distractorRationales.label: A
distractorRationales.text: Although a larger sample includes more people, its estimate varies less from sample to sample, so the margin of error is smaller.

distractorRationales.label: C
distractorRationales.text: The margin of error depends on the sample size, not only on the population.

distractorRationales.label: D
distractorRationales.text: Any sample smaller than the whole population leaves some uncertainty, so the margin of error is greater than zero.

content.stem: Two towns each surveyed a random sample of working adults about their one-way commute times. In Town A, the sample mean was $24$ minutes, with a margin of error of $3$ minutes. In Town B, the sample mean was $28$ minutes, with a margin of error of $3$ minutes. Which conclusion is most appropriate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The mean commute time of all working adults in Town B is greater than that in Town A.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The mean commute time of all working adults in Town B is exactly $4$ minutes greater than that in Town A.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Because the ranges of plausible values overlap, the surveys do not give convincing evidence that the mean commute times of all working adults in the two towns differ.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The mean commute time of all working adults in Town A is between $24$ and $27$ minutes.

content.explanation: Subtracting and adding the margin of error, the plausible values for Town A's mean are $24 - 3 = 21$ to $24 + 3 = 27$ minutes, and for Town B's mean, $28 - 3 = 25$ to $28 + 3 = 31$ minutes. These ranges overlap from $25$ to $27$, so it's possible that the two population means are equal (or even that Town A's is greater). The surveys don't support concluding that they differ.

distractorRationales.label: A
distractorRationales.text: Town B's sample mean is greater, but the plausible ranges overlap, so the population means could be equal.

distractorRationales.label: B
distractorRationales.text: The $4$-minute difference is between the sample means; the population means are not known exactly.

distractorRationales.label: D
distractorRationales.text: The plausible range for Town A is $24 - 3$ to $24 + 3$, or $21$ to $27$ minutes, not $24$ to $27$.

content.stem: A random sample of $500$ students was selected from all the high school students in one county. Of those surveyed, $70\%$ said they would prefer a later school start time, with a margin of error of $4$ percentage points. To which group can the survey's conclusion most reasonably be applied?

choices.label: A
choices.text: All high school students in the county

choices.label: B
choices.text: All high school students in the country

choices.label: C
choices.text: Only the $500$ students who were surveyed

choices.label: D
choices.text: All residents of the county

content.explanation: A random sample represents the population it was drawn from. The students were chosen from all high school students in the county, so the estimate (from $70\% - 4\% = 66\%$ to $70\% + 4\% = 74\%$) applies to that group.

distractorRationales.label: B
distractorRationales.text: The sample came only from one county, so it may not represent students elsewhere.

distractorRationales.label: C
distractorRationales.text: The point of a random sample is to estimate a larger population; for the $500$ students themselves, the percent is known exactly.

distractorRationales.label: D
distractorRationales.text: Only high school students were sampled, so the result doesn't represent adults or other residents.

content.stem: Based on a random sample of adults in a city, the mean nightly sleep of the city's adults is estimated to be $6.8$ hours, with a margin of error of $0.3$ hour at the $95\%$ confidence level. Which statement is the best interpretation of these results?

choices.label: A
choices.text: About $95\%$ of the adults in the city sleep between $6.5$ and $7.1$ hours per night.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is plausible that the mean nightly sleep of all adults in the city is between $6.5$ and $7.1$ hours.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Every adult in the city sleeps between $6.5$ and $7.1$ hours per night.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The mean nightly sleep of the adults in the sample is between $6.5$ and $7.1$ hours, but its exact value is unknown.

content.explanation: The margin of error describes uncertainty about a population mean, not about individuals. Plausible values for the mean sleep of all adults in the city are $6.8 - 0.3 = 6.5$ to $6.8 + 0.3 = 7.1$ hours.

distractorRationales.label: A
distractorRationales.text: The interval is about the mean of the population, not about where individual adults' sleep falls; individual sleep times vary much more.

distractorRationales.label: C
distractorRationales.text: Individual adults can sleep far more or less than the mean; the interval says nothing about each person.

distractorRationales.label: D
distractorRationales.text: The sample mean is known exactly: $6.8$ hours. The uncertainty is about the population mean.

content.stem: A ballot measure needs more than $50\%$ of the vote to pass. In a poll of a random sample of likely voters, $53\%$ said they support the measure, with a margin of error of $4$ percentage points. Assuming the likely voters vote as the poll indicates, which conclusion is best supported by the poll?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The measure will certainly pass.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A majority of likely voters support the measure, because $53\%$ is greater than $50\%$.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The poll results are consistent both with a majority supporting the measure and with less than half supporting it, so the poll does not show that a majority supports it.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Fewer than half of likely voters most likely support the measure.

content.explanation: The plausible range for support among all likely voters is $53\% - 4\% = 49\%$ to $53\% + 4\% = 57\%$. This range includes values above $50\%$ and values below $50\%$, so the poll can't establish that a majority supports the measure.

distractorRationales.label: A
distractorRationales.text: Values as low as $49\%$ are plausible, so passage is not certain.

distractorRationales.label: B
distractorRationales.text: $53\%$ is the sample estimate; the true support could be as low as $49\%$.

distractorRationales.label: D
distractorRationales.text: Most of the plausible range, $49\%$ to $57\%$, is above $50\%$; the poll gives no reason to think support is most likely below half.

content.stem: A town has $8{,}000$ households. In a random sample of $250$ of these households, $30\%$ had solar panels. The margin of error for this estimate is $5.5$ percentage points. Which of the following is the most plausible number of households in the town that have solar panels?
content.explanation: The plausible percent of all households with solar panels runs from $30\% - 5.5\% = 24.5\%$ to $30\% + 5.5\% = 35.5\%$. For $8{,}000$ households, that is $0.245 \times 8{,}000 = 1{,}960$ to $0.355 \times 8{,}000 = 2{,}840$ households. Only $2{,}600$ is in this range. (As a percent, $\frac{2{,}600}{8{,}000} = 0.325$, or $32.5\%$.)

distractorRationales.label: A
distractorRationales.text: This is $30\%$ of the $250$ sampled households, not an estimate for the whole town.

distractorRationales.label: B
distractorRationales.text: $1{,}600$ is $20\%$ of the households, below the lowest plausible value of $24.5\%$.

distractorRationales.label: D
distractorRationales.text: $3{,}000$ is $37.5\%$ of the households, above the highest plausible value of $35.5\%$.

content.stem: A wildlife biologist weighed a random sample of rainbow trout from a large lake. Based on the sample, the mean mass of all rainbow trout in the lake is estimated to be $1.4$ kilograms, with a margin of error of $0.2$ kilogram. Which of the following is NOT a plausible value for the mean mass, in kilograms, of all rainbow trout in the lake?
content.explanation: The plausible values for the mean mass of all the trout are the values within one margin of error of the estimate. Subtracting the margin of error from the estimate gives the lower end: $1.4 - 0.2 = 1.2$ kilograms. Adding the margin of error to the estimate gives the upper end: $1.4 + 0.2 = 1.6$ kilograms. So the plausible values run from $1.2$ to $1.6$ kilograms. Checking each choice: $1.25$, $1.35$ and $1.55$ are all between $1.2$ and $1.6$, so they are plausible. But $1.65$ is greater than the upper end, $1.6$, so it is NOT a plausible value.

distractorRationales.label: A
distractorRationales.text: $1.25$ is greater than the lower end of the range, $1.4 - 0.2 = 1.2$, so it is a plausible value.

distractorRationales.label: B
distractorRationales.text: $1.35$ is between $1.2$ and $1.6$, so it is a plausible value.

distractorRationales.label: C
distractorRationales.text: $1.55$ is less than the upper end of the range, $1.4 + 0.2 = 1.6$, so it is a plausible value.

content.stem: A polling firm surveyed a random sample of $900$ adults in a state and estimated, at the $90\%$ confidence level, that $44\%$ of the state's adults own a houseplant. Using the same sample data, the firm then calculated a margin of error at the $99\%$ confidence level. How does the margin of error at the $99\%$ confidence level compare with the margin of error at the $90\%$ confidence level?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It is smaller, because a higher confidence level means the estimate is more precise.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is larger, because being more confident that the range contains the population percent requires a wider range.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is the same, because the sample size did not change.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It cannot be compared, because a margin of error can be calculated at only one confidence level.

content.explanation: A confidence level describes how sure we are that the range of plausible values (the estimate plus or minus the margin of error) contains the true population value. To be more sure, the range has to be wider, so it has a better chance of catching the true value. With the same sample of $900$ adults, raising the confidence level from $90\%$ to $99\%$ therefore makes the margin of error larger.

distractorRationales.label: A
distractorRationales.text: This reverses the relationship. A higher confidence level does not make the estimate more precise; it makes the range wider so that we can be more sure it contains the population percent.

distractorRationales.label: C
distractorRationales.text: Sample size is only one thing that affects the margin of error. With the same sample, a higher confidence level still gives a larger margin of error.

distractorRationales.label: D
distractorRationales.text: The same sample data can be used to find a margin of error at any confidence level; higher levels simply give larger margins of error.

content.stem: A researcher measured the body lengths of a random sample of $50$ green frogs from a pond. The mean length of the frogs in the sample was $6.2$ centimeters. Based on the sample, the researcher estimated the mean length of all green frogs in the pond to be $6.2$ centimeters, with a margin of error of $0.4$ centimeter. Which statement must be true?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The mean length of the $50$ frogs in the sample is $6.2$ centimeters.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The mean length of all green frogs in the pond is $6.2$ centimeters.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Every green frog in the pond is between $5.8$ and $6.6$ centimeters long.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The mean length of all green frogs in the pond is between $5.8$ and $6.6$ centimeters.

content.explanation: The researcher actually measured the $50$ frogs in the sample, so their mean length, $6.2$ centimeters, is known exactly. The margin of error describes uncertainty about the population (all the frogs in the pond), not about the sample. Subtracting and adding the margin of error gives $6.2 - 0.4 = 5.8$ and $6.2 + 0.4 = 6.6$, so the population mean is plausibly between $5.8$ and $6.6$ centimeters, but this is not guaranteed. The only statement that must be true is the one about the sample.

distractorRationales.label: B
distractorRationales.text: The sample mean is only an estimate of the population mean. The population mean could be a different value, which is why there is a margin of error.

distractorRationales.label: C
distractorRationales.text: The margin of error is about the mean length, not about individual frogs. Individual frogs can be much shorter or longer than the mean.

distractorRationales.label: D
distractorRationales.text: The range from $5.8$ to $6.6$ centimeters contains the plausible values for the population mean, but it is not certain to contain it, so this statement does not have to be true.

content.stem: A city surveyed two independent random samples of residents about whether they support extending library hours. In the sample of residents ages $18$ to $29$, $64\%$ supported the change, with a margin of error of $5$ percentage points. In the sample of residents ages $65$ and older, $41\%$ supported the change, with a margin of error of $4$ percentage points. Which conclusion is most appropriate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Exactly $23\%$ more residents ages $18$ to $29$ than residents ages $65$ and older support the change.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The surveys do not give convincing evidence of a difference, because each estimate has a margin of error.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The percent of all city residents ages $18$ to $29$ who support the change is likely greater than the percent of all city residents ages $65$ and older who support it.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A majority of all city residents ages $65$ and older likely support the change.

content.explanation: Find the range of plausible values for each group by subtracting and adding its margin of error. For ages $18$ to $29$: $64\% - 5\% = 59\%$ and $64\% + 5\% = 69\%$, so the plausible range is $59\%$ to $69\%$. For ages $65$ and older: $41\% - 4\% = 37\%$ and $41\% + 4\% = 45\%$, so the plausible range is $37\%$ to $45\%$. The lowest plausible value for the younger group, $59\%$, is greater than the highest plausible value for the older group, $45\%$. Because the ranges do not overlap, it is reasonable to conclude that the percent of all younger residents who support the change is likely greater than the percent of all older residents who support it.

distractorRationales.label: A
distractorRationales.text: $64 - 41 = 23$ is the difference between the sample percents, but the population percents are uncertain, so the difference is not known exactly. (It is also a difference in percentage points, not "$23\%$ more residents.")

distractorRationales.label: B
distractorRationales.text: Having a margin of error does not rule out a conclusion. Here the two ranges, $59\%$ to $69\%$ and $37\%$ to $45\%$, do not overlap, so the data do give convincing evidence of a difference.

distractorRationales.label: D
distractorRationales.text: For residents ages $65$ and older, every plausible value from $37\%$ to $45\%$ is below $50\%$, so a majority likely does not support the change.

content.stem: A forest contains $6{,}500$ ash trees. Foresters inspected a random sample of $200$ of these trees and found that $18\%$ of them were infested with a beetle. The margin of error for this estimate is $5$ percentage points. Which of the following gives the most plausible range for the number of ash trees in the forest that are infested?
content.explanation: First, find the range of plausible percents for the whole forest. Subtracting the margin of error from the sample percent gives $18\% - 5\% = 13\%$. Adding it gives $18\% + 5\% = 23\%$. So between $13\%$ and $23\%$ of all $6{,}500$ ash trees are plausibly infested. Next, convert each percent to a number of trees by multiplying by $6{,}500$. For the lower end, $13\% = 0.13$, and $0.13 \times 6{,}500 = 845$. For the upper end, $23\% = 0.23$, and $0.23 \times 6{,}500 = 1{,}495$. So the most plausible range is $845$ to $1{,}495$ infested trees.

distractorRationales.label: A
distractorRationales.text: This applies the percents to the $200$ sampled trees ($0.13 \times 200 = 26$ and $0.23 \times 200 = 46$) instead of to all $6{,}500$ trees in the forest.

distractorRationales.label: C
distractorRationales.text: This finds the point estimate $0.18 \times 6{,}500 = 1{,}170$ and then subtracts and adds $5$ trees. The margin of error is $5$ percentage points, which is $0.05 \times 6{,}500 = 325$ trees, not $5$ trees.

distractorRationales.label: D
distractorRationales.text: This uses the point estimate, $1{,}170$, as the lower end. The lower end should be found by subtracting the margin of error: $0.13 \times 6{,}500 = 845$.

content.stem: A news report about a random survey of a county's high school seniors states, "It is plausible that between $38\%$ and $46\%$ of all seniors in the county plan to attend college outside the state." The range of plausible values was found by subtracting the margin of error from, and adding it to, the percent found in the sample. What were the sample percent and the margin of error?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Sample percent: $38\%$; margin of error: $8$ percentage points

choices.label: B
choices.text: Sample percent: $46\%$; margin of error: $8$ percentage points

choices.label: C
choices.text: Sample percent: $42\%$; margin of error: $4$ percentage points

choices.label: D
choices.text: Sample percent: $42\%$; margin of error: $8$ percentage points

content.explanation: The sample percent is in the middle of the range, so it is the average of the two ends. Adding the ends gives $38 + 46 = 84$, and dividing by $2$ gives $84 \div 2 = 42$, so the sample percent is $42\%$. The margin of error is the distance from the middle to either end: $46 - 42 = 4$ (and also $42 - 38 = 4$). So the margin of error is $4$ percentage points. Check: $42\% - 4\% = 38\%$ and $42\% + 4\% = 46\%$, which matches the report.

distractorRationales.label: A
distractorRationales.text: $38\%$ is the lower end of the range, not the sample percent, and $8$ is the width of the whole range ($46 - 38 = 8$), which is twice the margin of error.

distractorRationales.label: B
distractorRationales.text: $46\%$ is the upper end of the range, not the sample percent, and $8$ is the full width of the range rather than the margin of error.

distractorRationales.label: D
distractorRationales.text: The sample percent is correct, but $8$ is the full width of the range. The margin of error is half of that, $8 \div 2 = 4$, because it is added on one side and subtracted on the other.

content.stem: A company claims that the mean battery life of its wireless earbuds is $10$ hours. An independent lab tested a random sample of $40$ pairs of the earbuds and found a mean battery life of $9.4$ hours, with a margin of error of $0.3$ hour. Which conclusion is best supported by the lab's results?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The company's claim is likely too high, because $10$ hours is outside the range of plausible values for the mean battery life of all the earbuds.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The company's claim is supported, because $9.4$ hours is close to $10$ hours.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The company's claim is likely too low, because some pairs in the sample lasted longer than $10$ hours.

choices.label: D
choices.text: No conclusion about the claim can be drawn, because only $40$ pairs of earbuds were tested.

content.explanation: Find the range of plausible values for the mean battery life of all the earbuds. Subtracting the margin of error gives $9.4 - 0.3 = 9.1$ hours, and adding it gives $9.4 + 0.3 = 9.7$ hours. So the plausible values are from $9.1$ to $9.7$ hours. The claimed mean, $10$ hours, is greater than the highest plausible value, $9.7$ hours. So the lab's results suggest that the true mean is less than $10$ hours, which means the claim is likely too high.

distractorRationales.label: B
distractorRationales.text: Being close is not enough. The plausible values run only from $9.1$ to $9.7$ hours, and $10$ hours is outside that range.

distractorRationales.label: C
distractorRationales.text: The claim is about the mean battery life. Individual pairs lasting longer than $10$ hours does not change the fact that every plausible value for the mean is below $10$.

distractorRationales.label: D
distractorRationales.text: A random sample of $40$ pairs is enough to give an estimate with a margin of error; the margin of error already accounts for the sample size, and it shows that $10$ hours is not plausible.

content.stem: To estimate the percent of a city's households that compost food scraps, researchers randomly selected $2{,}000$ households from a complete list of the city's households and mailed each one a survey. Only $400$ of the selected households returned the survey. Of those, $31\%$ said they compost, and the researchers reported a margin of error of $5$ percentage points. Which statement best describes a limitation of this estimate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The margin of error should be $0$, because the households were chosen at random from a complete list.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The estimate cannot apply to the city, because $400$ households is less than $1\%$ of all households in a large city.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The true percent must be between $26\%$ and $36\%$, because the households were chosen at random.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Households that chose to return the survey may differ from those that did not, and the margin of error does not account for that possible bias.

content.explanation: A margin of error measures only the uncertainty that comes from random sampling: the chance that a random sample does not perfectly match the population. It does not measure bias. Here, only $400$ of the $2{,}000$ selected households responded. Dividing, $400 \div 2{,}000 = 0.2$, so only $20\%$ of the selected households responded. Households that care about composting may be more likely to return a survey about it, so the people who responded may not represent all households. If so, the true percent could be outside the reported range of $31\% - 5\% = 26\%$ to $31\% + 5\% = 36\%$, and the margin of error would not reveal that.

distractorRationales.label: A
distractorRationales.text: Random selection does not make an estimate exact. Any sample has some sampling error, so the margin of error is greater than $0$.

distractorRationales.label: B
distractorRationales.text: A random sample can be a small fraction of a population and still give a useful estimate. The problem here is who responded, not the fraction of the city that was sampled.

distractorRationales.label: C
distractorRationales.text: Even with perfect random sampling, the range of plausible values is not guaranteed to contain the true value. And here, because so many households did not respond, the estimate may also be biased.

content.stem: A random sample of $1{,}200$ adults in a country was surveyed, and $61\%$ said they read the news online daily, with a margin of error of $3$ percentage points. Among the $150$ adults in the sample who are teachers, $70\%$ said they read the news online daily. Which statement about an estimate for all teachers in the country, based only on the $150$ teachers in the sample, is most likely true?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Its margin of error would be $3$ percentage points, the same as for the whole survey.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Its margin of error would be less than $3$ percentage points, because teachers are a more similar group.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Its margin of error would be greater than $3$ percentage points, because it is based on a smaller number of people.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It would have no margin of error, because the $150$ teachers are a subgroup rather than a random sample.

content.explanation: The margin of error depends on how many people an estimate is based on: smaller samples give less precise estimates and so larger margins of error. The estimate for the whole adult population uses all $1{,}200$ people, and its margin of error is $3$ percentage points. The estimate for teachers uses only the $150$ teachers, which is $\frac{150}{1{,}200} = \frac{1}{8}$ of the sample. With far fewer people, the estimate for teachers is less precise, so its margin of error would be greater than $3$ percentage points.

distractorRationales.label: A
distractorRationales.text: The $3$-point margin of error goes with the estimate based on all $1{,}200$ adults. An estimate based on only $150$ people is less precise.

distractorRationales.label: B
distractorRationales.text: Even if teachers' answers were somewhat similar, the much smaller number of people would make the estimate less precise, not more.

distractorRationales.label: D
distractorRationales.text: The teachers in a random sample of adults are a random sample of teachers, so an estimate for teachers still has sampling uncertainty and a margin of error.

content.stem: Two polling firms each surveyed a different random sample of the registered voters in the same state, using the same question, during the same week. Firm X found that $52\%$ supported a proposed tax, with a margin of error of $3$ percentage points. Firm Y found that $47\%$ supported the tax, with a margin of error of $3$ percentage points. Which statement best explains how both results could be accurate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Because the ranges of plausible values overlap, both results are consistent with the same population percent, such as $49.5\%$; the difference can be explained by random variation between samples.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Both results cannot be accurate, because the two sample percents are different.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Both results are accurate only if exactly $49.5\%$ of the state's registered voters support the tax.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Both results could be accurate only if the two firms surveyed different populations.

content.explanation: Find each firm's range of plausible values. For Firm X: $52\% - 3\% = 49\%$ and $52\% + 3\% = 55\%$, so its range is $49\%$ to $55\%$. For Firm Y: $47\% - 3\% = 44\%$ and $47\% + 3\% = 50\%$, so its range is $44\%$ to $50\%$. The ranges overlap from $49\%$ to $50\%$. Any population percent in that overlap, such as $49.5\%$, is plausible according to both polls. Different random samples from the same population naturally give somewhat different results, so the two polls do not contradict each other.

distractorRationales.label: B
distractorRationales.text: Different random samples from the same population almost always give different sample percents. That is why each estimate has a margin of error.

distractorRationales.label: C
distractorRationales.text: $49.5\%$ is just one value in the overlap. Any value from $49\%$ to $50\%$ would be consistent with both polls.

distractorRationales.label: D
distractorRationales.text: Both firms sampled the same population. Their results differ because of random sampling variation, which the overlapping ranges allow for.
